summary:
A trans visitor to Chad faces formal criminal exposure. The penal code in force since 1 August 2017 criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults under Article 354, carrying three months to two years' imprisonment and fines of 50,000 to 500,000 CFA francs (approximately 89 to 885 US dollars). The US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Practices report on Chad confirms this as the operative legal position, and a trans person whose conduct or relationships are read as same-sex falls under the provision. The National Assembly adopted the code on 12 December 2016 by 111 votes to one with four abstentions, after a criminalisation drive that succeeded in Chad and Nigeria while comparable further attempts failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda.

Chad has no legal gender recognition, so there is no pathway for a person to amend sex markers on official documents. A trans visitor carrying documents that do not match presentation has no domestic remedy available, and the state provides no framework under which such a mismatch could be regularised before or during travel.

The pre-criminalisation baseline was ambiguity rather than permission. The US State Department's 2010 report on Chad recorded that the law prohibited but did not define "unnatural acts", and found no evidence that year that the provision had been used against LGBT persons; it also documented no known LGBT organisations and few reports of violence, with most persons discreet because of social strictures. The 2013 arrests of two gay men in Abéché for celebrating a wedding, which occurred before the penal code formally outlawed homosexuality, illustrate how that ambiguity was already being enforced: the bar was ordered closed for two years, both men were fined and initially received two-year prison sentences, and community outcry followed when the sentences were suspended on appeal.

Protection machinery is thin and in some respects operates against the victim. There is no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. Because homosexuality is criminalised, authorities refuse to investigate or prosecute crimes committed against LGBTQ+ people, and local civil society members report that dozens of LGBTQ+ people are imprisoned under the pretext of other charges. The single exception in the penal code is Article 350(i), which imposes ten to twenty years' imprisonment where rape is committed because of the victim's sexual orientation, a provision whose practical use against trans or LGBT victims is not documented in the sources.

A separate provision, Article 360, sits in Chapter III on sexual offences against minors: it punishes anyone who, without violence, maintains a sexual relationship or practices sexual touching on a person of the same sex under eighteen years of age with one to three years' imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 500,000 francs (approximately 177 to 885 US dollars).

Social conditions push concealment. The US State Department's 2023 report states that LGBTQ+ people continue to hide their identity to protect their safety. Chadian activists report that social and familial pressure is used to coerce LGBTQ+ people into changing their sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression, and LGBTQ+ people face difficulty obtaining housing, employment, and government services. In a 2024 survey, only 15 percent of Chadians felt their local area would be a good place for gay and lesbian people to live.
tangentialFactors:
Chad's formal legal architecture offers few entry points for a trans visitor seeking redress. No laws formally restrict LGBTQ+ people's freedom of expression, association, or peaceful assembly, but discrimination and marginalisation effectively limit these rights in practice, meaning the formal absence of an assembly ban is not a reliable indicator of safety at a public event or gathering.

Political and religious framing shapes enforcement. A former Prime Minister, Delwa Kassiré Coumakoye, defended the 2017 criminalisation law on religious grounds, stating that homosexuality is condemned by all religions. LGBTQ+ people are societally viewed as threats to family, procreation, and marriage, and homosexuality is perceived as a Western invention, a framing that can attach格外 scrutiny to foreign visitors whose presentation is read as gender-nonconforming.

Despite constitutional universal suffrage, LGBTQ+ people are often denied voter registration by local authorities, evidencing that administrative discretion is routinely used to exclude. Men who have sex with men are unlikely to be able to donate blood, not because of a formal ban but because of discrimination and hostility when accessing healthcare, which indicates the treatment setting itself carries an outing risk.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the concealment requirement rather than a periodic enforcement campaign. Activists describe social and familial pressure to change sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression, and LGBTQ+ Chadians have documented difficulty securing housing, employment, and government services, with no anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

Family formation is closed. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Chad, and same-sex couples cannot adopt children together. Single people may adopt, but this requires a social services investigation that includes an inquiry into the applicant's moral standing, which can be used as grounds to deny adoption and, by local accounts, can be weaponised against LGBTQ+ applicants.

Public opinion data supports the concealment norm: a 2024 survey found that only 15 percent of Chadians believed their local area would be a good place for gay and lesbian people to live, and youth associations were among the groups that petitioned the government to punish the two men arrested in Abéché in 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
Three items remain unresolved in the sources and should be treated as gaps rather than findings. First, no source in the inventory documents how Chad's border or airport authorities handle passport sex markers, secondary screening, or refusal of entry on gender-presentation grounds, so the entry-screening layer of visitor risk is not sourced. Second, the figure of dozens of LGBTQ+ people imprisoned under pretextual charges is attributed to local civil society members without a named organisation, a case list, or a date range, and is not independently corroborated elsewhere in the inventory. Third, the practical application of Article 350(i) — whether the sexual-orientation-motivated rape aggravation has ever been charged in favour of an LGBT or trans victim — is not documented.

One source in the inventory, the US State Department's 2006 Human Rights Practices report on Chad, documents Deby-regime abuses including extrajudicial killings and torture and the withdrawal of MINURCAT, but contains no trans-specific or sexual-orientation-specific finding. It therefore establishes only the general human-rights character of the state apparatus and is not cited for any claim about trans visitor exposure.
